basal-body-temperature.title: Basal body temperature
basal-body-temperature.glance: Basal body temperature is your at-rest morning temperature, which rises slightly after ovulation.
basal-body-temperature.overview:
Basal body temperature (BBT) is your body's temperature fully at rest. Measured the same way each
day, it shows a small but telling change across the cycle: after ovulation, it rises a little and
stays up until your next period.

The rise is small — around 0.4 to 0.8°F (roughly 0.2 to 0.4°C) — so it's read from a pattern over
several days, not a single reading. To catch it, you take your temperature each morning before
getting up, eating or drinking, ideally at the same time. Almost everyone has ovulated within about
three days of the temperature climbing.

Because the rise comes *after* the egg is released, BBT confirms that ovulation has happened rather
than predicting it in advance. Over a few cycles it can help you see the shape of your own cycle,
though on its own it isn't a precise way to catch the fertile days.
basal-body-temperature.deep:
BBT is one of the fertility-awareness signs recorded daily, together with cervical mucus and cycle
length. It pairs naturally with mucus tracking: the change to clear, slippery mucus suggests the
fertile window is opening, while the temperature rise a few days later confirms ovulation has
passed. Many things can nudge a resting temperature — poor sleep, illness, alcohol, or a lie-in —
so single odd readings matter less than the overall trend.

cervical-mucus.title: Cervical mucus
cervical-mucus.glance: Cervical mucus is the natural discharge that changes through the cycle and marks your fertile days.
cervical-mucus.overview:
Cervical mucus is the fluid the cervix makes, which you may notice as discharge. It's normal, and
its look and feel change in a fairly predictable pattern across the cycle — which is why it's one
of the signs used to spot the fertile days.

Just after a period there are often a few "dry" days with little mucus. As an egg begins to
mature, mucus increases and tends to be white or yellow, cloudy and sticky. In the days right
before ovulation it usually turns clear, wet and slippery, stretching between the fingers like raw
egg white — this is the most fertile time. After ovulation it typically becomes sticky and cloudy
again, or dries up.

Everyone's pattern is a little different, and it can take a few cycles of paying attention to learn
your own. Some things — such as hormonal contraception, breastfeeding, or an infection — can change
the mucus, so it isn't a reliable fertility sign for everyone.
cervical-mucus.deep:
Reading cervical mucus is one of the fertility-awareness signs people track, alongside resting body
temperature and cycle length; learning them usually takes two to three cycles. Unlike a temperature
rise, which confirms ovulation only after it has happened, the shift to clear, slippery, egg-white
mucus tends to appear *before* ovulation, which is why it's used to flag the fertile window as it
opens rather than after it closes.

endometriosis.title: Endometriosis
endometriosis.glance: Endometriosis is a condition where tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb, often causing pain.
endometriosis.overview:
Endometriosis is a long-term condition where cells similar to the lining of the womb (uterus) grow
in other parts of the body, such as around the ovaries, the pelvis, or the bowel. It's common —
estimated to affect around 1 in 10 women of reproductive age worldwide.

Because this tissue behaves a little like the womb lining, it can cause inflammation and, over time,
scar tissue. The most common sign is pain: often severe period pain, but also pelvic or lower-back
pain at other times, pain during or after sex, and pain when peeing or pooing. Very heavy periods,
deep tiredness, low mood, and difficulty getting pregnant are also common. Symptoms vary a lot —
some people have severe pain, others little.

Endometriosis is often misunderstood and can take years to recognise, partly because period pain is
so often dismissed as "normal." Severe pain that disrupts your life is not something you simply have
to put up with — it's worth taking seriously.
endometriosis.deep:
The exact cause of endometriosis isn't known, and there's currently no cure — but treatments can
help manage the symptoms, and support ranges from medicines to, for some people, surgery, alongside
help for the physical and emotional toll. One of the biggest challenges is delay: on average it can
take several years, sometimes many, to reach a diagnosis. That's part of why keeping a clear record
of your symptoms, and returning to a clinician if you're not being heard, can matter so much.
endometriosis.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth seeing a GP if:

- you have severe period pain that stops you doing normal activities
- your periods are very heavy — for example, needing to change a pad or tampon every 1–2 hours
- you have ongoing pelvic or lower-back pain, pain during or after sex, or pain when peeing or pooing
- you're finding it hard to get pregnant
- treatment you've already had hasn't helped, or your symptoms have got worse

Because endometriosis can take time to diagnose, it's okay to go back if your symptoms aren't taken
seriously — a clear picture of your pain over time helps. If the pain or heavy bleeding is also
affecting your mood, tell your GP; that's part of the picture, and support is available.

estrogen.title: Estrogen
estrogen.glance: Estrogen is a key hormone that helps prepare your body for a possible pregnancy each cycle.
estrogen.overview:
Estrogen is one of the main hormones behind the menstrual cycle. In the first half of the cycle
(the follicular phase) its level rises as a follicle in the ovary matures. This rise thickens the
lining of the uterus and leads up to ovulation.

Estrogen also influences things you might notice day to day — energy, mood, and changes in
cervical mucus around your fertile days. After ovulation its level dips and then shifts again,
working alongside another hormone, progesterone, through the second half of the cycle.

Levels naturally rise and fall across each cycle, and they change across life stages too. This is
normal — it's the rhythm your body runs on, not something to "fix."
estrogen.deep:
Estrogen isn't a single substance but a group of related hormones (the most active in the cycle
is estradiol). Most of it is made by the ovaries, in the growing follicle. Its cyclical rise and
fall — together with progesterone, and the brain's signalling hormones LH and FSH — is what
drives the phases of the cycle. Because estrogen touches many systems, its natural shifts can
show up in small ways throughout the month; tracking helps you learn your own pattern rather than
compare it to an "average."

fertile-window.title: The fertile window
fertile-window.glance: The fertile window is the handful of days each cycle when sex can lead to pregnancy.
fertile-window.overview:
The fertile window is the short stretch of the cycle when pregnancy is possible. It exists because
of two timings that don't quite line up: an egg can only be fertilised for about 12 to 24 hours
after it's released, but sperm can survive inside the body for several days — up to about a week —
waiting for an egg.

Put together, that means the window opens a few days before ovulation and closes about a day
after it. In practice you're most fertile in the 2 to 3 days leading up to ovulation and on the
day itself, because sperm can already be there when the egg arrives.

Since ovulation can shift from cycle to cycle, the fertile window moves too. That's why it's
usually thought of as a range of days rather than a single date, and why tracking signs across
several cycles is more dependable than counting on one calendar calculation.
fertile-window.deep:
The exact days differ from person to person and month to month, so the window is best estimated
from the body's own signals rather than a fixed formula. Changes in cervical mucus point to the
window opening as ovulation approaches, and a rise in resting body temperature confirms — after
the fact — that ovulation has passed and the window has closed. Ovulation predictor kits work a
step earlier, detecting the surge in luteinizing hormone (LH) that comes shortly before the egg is
released.

first-period.title: Starting periods (first period)
first-period.glance: Your first period usually arrives around age 12 — anywhere from about 8 to 17 is normal.
first-period.overview:
Your first period — sometimes called menarche — is when the menstrual cycle begins for the first
time. Most people start around age 12, but anywhere from about 8 to 17 is normal. It often comes
roughly two years after your breasts start to develop.

There are usually signs in the lead-up: growing underarm and pubic hair, and a little clear or
white discharge in the months before. Knowing these are coming can make the first period feel less
sudden.

At the start, periods are often irregular — the gaps can be long or short, and it can take your
body several months, even a couple of years, to settle into a steadier rhythm. Once it does,
periods tend to come somewhere around every 23 to 35 days and last about 2 to 7 days. Early
irregularity is normal and not something to worry about.
first-period.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP if periods **have not started by age 15**, or by **13 if there are no other signs of
  puberty** (like breast development or body hair). This is just to check things are developing as
  expected — usually everything is fine.

follicular-phase.title: Follicular phase
follicular-phase.glance: The follicular phase is the first half of the cycle, when an egg ripens and the womb lining thickens.
follicular-phase.overview:
The follicular phase is the first part of the cycle. It begins on the first day of your period and
runs up to ovulation. Its name comes from the follicle — the small fluid-filled sac in the ovary
that holds and grows an egg during this time.

Through this phase the hormone estrogen rises. That rising estrogen does two main things: it helps
a follicle in the ovary mature, and it thickens the lining of the uterus (womb), getting the body
ready in case a pregnancy begins later in the cycle.

Because estrogen is climbing, some people notice more energy or changes in cervical mucus as the
fertile days approach. Everyone's experience is different, and none of it needs "managing" — it's
simply the first half of your cycle doing its work.
follicular-phase.deep:
The follicular phase can vary in length from cycle to cycle, which is part of why whole cycles
differ from person to person and month to month. It ends when rising estrogen helps trigger the
release of an egg (ovulation). Because its final days lead into ovulation, this is when the fertile
window opens — which is why the end of the follicular phase matters for anyone tracking fertility.

fsh.title: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
fsh.glance: FSH is a brain hormone that prompts follicles in the ovary to grow at the start of each cycle.
fsh.overview:
FSH — follicle-stimulating hormone — is one of the messenger hormones that get the cycle going.
It's made by a small gland in the brain (the pituitary) and, as its name says, it stimulates
follicles: the tiny fluid-filled sacs in the ovary that each hold an egg.

Early in the cycle, FSH encourages a group of these follicles to start growing. As a follicle
develops it releases more estrogen, which in turn thickens the lining of the uterus (womb) ready
for a possible pregnancy. Usually one follicle becomes the dominant one that goes on toward
ovulation.

FSH rises and falls as part of the normal back-and-forth of the cycle. You don't feel FSH directly
— it works quietly in the background, setting up the more visible changes of the follicular phase.
fsh.deep:
FSH works as a pair with luteinizing hormone (LH); both are released by the pituitary gland in the
brain and together they drive the ovaries through the cycle. FSH leads the first half, growing the
follicles, while the LH surge later marks the mid-cycle release of an egg. This partnership is also
why fertility treatments use FSH-based medicines: giving extra FSH encourages several follicles to
mature at once, rather than the single one a natural cycle usually produces.

lh.title: Luteinizing hormone (LH)
lh.glance: LH is the brain hormone whose mid-cycle surge triggers the ovary to release an egg.
lh.overview:
LH — luteinizing hormone — is the messenger that sets off ovulation. Like FSH, it's made by a
small gland in the brain (the pituitary) and it tells the ovary when to release an egg.

For most of the first half of the cycle LH stays low. Then, around the middle of the cycle, it
rises sharply in what's called the LH surge. This surge is the signal that causes the ovary to
release its egg — ovulation — usually a day or so later.

The surge is a brief, well-timed signal rather than something you'd notice in how you feel. Because
it comes so closely before the egg is released, the timing of the LH rise is a reliable marker of
the most fertile part of the cycle.
lh.deep:
LH works together with FSH, the hormone that grows the follicles earlier in the cycle. Where FSH
leads the build-up, the LH surge is the turning point: levels begin climbing roughly a day and a
half before the egg is released and peak about half a day before it. After the surge, the cycle
moves into its second half. This tight timing is why LH is such a useful marker for anyone tracking
ovulation, and why it's central to how fertility treatments are planned.

luteal-phase.title: Luteal phase
luteal-phase.glance: The luteal phase is the second half of the cycle, after ovulation, when progesterone rises.
luteal-phase.overview:
The luteal phase is the part of the cycle that follows ovulation and runs until your next period
begins. It's named after the corpus luteum — the small structure the ovary forms from the empty
follicle once the egg has been released.

In this phase the hormone progesterone rises. Its job is to keep the lining of the uterus (womb)
thick and settled, so that if a fertilised egg arrives it has somewhere to implant. Estrogen stays
part of the picture too, working alongside progesterone.

If no pregnancy begins, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone and estrogen fall, and the
lining is no longer maintained — which brings on your next period and starts a new cycle. This is
also the stretch when some people notice premenstrual changes in mood, sleep or the body.
luteal-phase.deep:
The luteal phase tends to be a little steadier in length than the first half of the cycle, often
running somewhere in the region of about two weeks, though there's normal variation from person to
person. Because its end is tied to the fall in progesterone, the arrival of a period is really the
visible sign that hormone levels have dropped. Tracking how you feel across the luteal phase can
help you tell apart what's a familiar pattern for you from what's new or worth a conversation with
a clinician.

menopause.title: Menopause
menopause.glance: Menopause is when periods stop for good — a natural stage, usually reached between about 45 and 55.
menopause.overview:
Menopause is the point when your periods stop permanently. Because periods can come and go for a
while first, it's counted as reached once you've gone 12 months in a row without one. It usually
happens between about 45 and 55, though it can be earlier or later.

It's a natural part of ageing, not an illness. It happens as the ovaries wind down and the level of
estrogen — a key hormone of the cycle — falls. That hormonal shift is behind the changes many
people notice: hot flushes and night sweats, changes to periods in the lead-up, trouble sleeping,
shifts in mood or anxiety, brain fog, vaginal dryness, and aches.

Experiences vary enormously — some people sail through, others find it hard, and symptoms can last
several years. None of it means something is wrong with you. Support and options exist, and
understanding what's happening is a good first step.
menopause.deep:
The years of change leading up to menopause are called perimenopause; menopause itself is a single
point in time (that 12-months-without-a-period mark), and the time after is sometimes called
postmenopause. Because estrogen also affects bones and the heart over the long term, clinicians pay
attention to those alongside day-to-day symptoms. A range of approaches — from lifestyle to
non-hormonal and hormonal treatments — can ease symptoms, and what's right depends on your health,
history and preferences, which is a conversation to have with a clinician.
menopause.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP if menopause symptoms are troubling you or affecting daily life, and you'd like to talk
  through your options.
- **Always** see a GP if you have **any vaginal bleeding after 12 months without a period**
  (bleeding after menopause). It's often nothing serious, but it should always be checked.
- It's also worth checking in if you're bleeding more rather than less than before, or your periods
  change in a way that worries you.

menstrual-cycle.title: The menstrual cycle
menstrual-cycle.glance: The menstrual cycle is the monthly rhythm your body runs on to prepare for a possible pregnancy.
menstrual-cycle.overview:
The menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of your period — that's day 1 — up to the day
before your next period starts. It's driven by hormones that rise and fall in a repeating pattern
each month.

A cycle is often around 28 days, but that's just an average. Anywhere from about 21 to 35 days is
normal, and your own length can vary a little from month to month. Learning your own pattern is
more useful than comparing it to a number.

Across the cycle your body moves through a few stages: your period, the build-up to releasing an
egg, the release itself (ovulation), and the stretch afterwards. Each stage is shaped by
hormones, mainly estrogen and progesterone.
menstrual-cycle.deep:
The whole cycle is a conversation between the brain and the ovaries, carried by hormones. In the
first half, estrogen rises as an egg-containing follicle matures in the ovary and the lining of
the uterus (womb) thickens. Around the middle of the cycle an egg is released. In the second half,
progesterone helps keep that lining ready in case a fertilised egg arrives.

If there's no pregnancy, estrogen and progesterone fall to low levels, the lining is shed as your
period, and the pattern begins again. Because these hormones touch many systems, you may notice
small day-to-day changes across the month — this is the normal rhythm of the cycle, not something
to "fix."

menstrual-phase.title: Menstrual phase (your period)
menstrual-phase.glance: Your period is the few days of bleeding that begin each cycle, as the womb lining is shed.
menstrual-phase.overview:
The menstrual phase is your period — the days when you bleed. It starts on day 1 of the cycle,
when the levels of estrogen and progesterone have dropped low enough that the lining built up
inside the uterus (womb) is no longer maintained and comes away, leaving the body through the
vagina.

A period usually lasts about 2 to 7 days, with roughly 5 days being typical. Flow is often
heaviest in the first couple of days and lighter after that. Periods commonly begin around age 12,
though starting earlier or later is also normal.

What's "normal" varies a lot from person to person. Tracking your own periods helps you notice
what's usual for you, which is far more meaningful than any average.
menstrual-phase.deep:
The bleeding of a period is the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) being shed after a cycle
where no pregnancy has begun. It marks both the end of one cycle and the start of the next, which
is why day 1 of your period is counted as day 1 of the whole cycle. As your period finishes,
estrogen begins to rise again and the body starts rebuilding the lining for the cycle ahead.

ovulation.title: Ovulation
ovulation.glance: Ovulation is when an ovary releases an egg — the most fertile point of your cycle.
ovulation.overview:
Ovulation is the moment an ovary releases a mature egg. It's the turning point of the cycle: the
first half builds up to it, and the second half follows it.

In a cycle of about 28 days, ovulation often happens around day 14 — but the timing varies. A
helpful way to think about it is that ovulation usually occurs somewhere from 10 to 16 days before
your next period starts. It can be hard to pinpoint the exact day.

Once released, an egg can be fertilised for only about 12 to 24 hours. Sperm, though, can survive
in the body for several days, so the "fertile window" is wider than a single day — roughly the few
days leading up to ovulation and the day itself.
ovulation.deep:
The release of the egg is triggered by a short, sharp rise in hormones around mid-cycle, following
the estrogen build-up of the follicular phase. Because sperm can live for a number of days while
the egg lives less than a day, pregnancy is most likely from sex in the days just before
ovulation. Ovulation can shift from cycle to cycle with things like stress or illness, which is
why predicting it exactly is difficult and why tracking several cycles is more reliable than any
single calculation.

pcos.title: PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome)
pcos.glance: PCOS is a common hormonal condition that can affect periods, ovulation, skin and hair.
pcos.overview:
PCOS — polycystic ovary syndrome — is a common condition linked to the balance of reproductive
hormones. Estimates suggest it affects somewhere around 1 in 10 women of reproductive age, and many
people who have it are never diagnosed.

It can show up in different ways, and no two people are quite the same. Common features include
periods that are irregular, infrequent, or absent; higher levels of hormones called androgens,
which can lead to extra hair growth on the face or body, acne, or thinning hair on the scalp; and
ovaries that don't release an egg as regularly as usual, which can make it harder to conceive.
Weight changes and patches of darker skin are also common.

The exact cause isn't fully understood, and there's no cure — but the symptoms can be managed, and
understanding what's happening is the first step. PCOS is common and manageable, not something to
feel ashamed of.
pcos.deep:
Because PCOS involves the body's hormones and how it handles insulin, it's also linked over the
longer term to insulin resistance and a higher chance of type 2 diabetes, raised blood pressure,
and changes in cholesterol — which is why clinicians tend to keep an eye on these things over time.
Roughly half of people with PCOS may develop diabetes or pre-diabetes by their forties, so regular
check-ins matter. Diagnosis isn't something to self-assess: a clinician looks at the overall
picture — your history and periods, sometimes blood tests for hormones, and sometimes an ultrasound
of the ovaries — and rules out other causes before reaching PCOS.
pcos.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth seeing a GP if you notice things that fit the picture above, especially if they're
affecting how you feel day to day:

- periods that are irregular, very infrequent, or have stopped
- noticeably more hair growth on the face or body, persistent acne, or scalp hair thinning
- difficulty getting pregnant after trying for a while
- weight gain that's hard to shift, alongside other symptoms

A GP can look into what's going on, confirm whether it's PCOS or something else, and talk through a
plan that fits you. PCOS is also linked with low mood and anxiety — if you're struggling with how
you feel, tell your GP too; that's part of the picture and support is available.

perimenopause.title: Perimenopause
perimenopause.glance: Perimenopause is the transition leading up to menopause, when periods and hormones start to change.
perimenopause.overview:
Perimenopause is the stretch of time leading up to menopause — the "around menopause" years. It
begins when you first notice the changes and runs until a full year after your last period, at
which point you've reached menopause. It can last several years.

During this time the ovaries gradually make less estrogen, and levels rise and fall less
predictably than before. The most common early sign is that periods change — becoming closer
together or further apart, lighter or heavier. Many of the symptoms linked with menopause, such as
hot flushes, sleep changes, or shifts in mood, can begin here while you're still having periods.

Because it's gradual and varies so much, perimenopause can be confusing — the changes don't arrive
all at once or in the same order for everyone. Knowing this phase has a name, and that it's a
normal transition, can make it easier to make sense of.
perimenopause.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP if perimenopause symptoms are affecting your daily life and you'd like to talk through
  what might help.
- It's worth getting checked if your periods become very heavy, or if you have bleeding between
  periods or after sex, so the cause can be found.
- Remember that pregnancy can still happen during perimenopause, so it's worth raising
  contraception with a clinician if that's relevant for you.

period-pain.title: Period pain
period-pain.glance: Period pain is cramping in your lower tummy around your period — common, and often a normal part of the cycle.
period-pain.overview:
Period pain is the cramping, aching feeling in your lower tummy that many people get around their
period. It happens when the muscular wall of the womb tightens, and it's often a normal part of the
menstrual cycle. The medical name for it is dysmenorrhea.

It usually comes on at the start of your period, or just before, and tends to last up to about
three days. For some it's a mild heaviness; for others the cramps are stronger. Pain can also
change over your life and from cycle to cycle.

Period pain that follows this familiar pattern is common and usually manageable. Everyday comfort
measures and simple painkillers are what many people use, and a pharmacist or GP can advise on what
might suit you. What matters is knowing your own usual pattern — so you can notice if something
changes.
period-pain.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth talking to a GP if:

- your periods become more painful, heavier, or more irregular than usual
- the pain stops you doing everyday things like work or school
- ordinary painkillers don't help
- you have pain during sex, or when peeing or pooing
- you bleed between periods
- your pain comes at times other than just before or during your period
- you pass blood clots larger than a coin (about the size of a quarter)
- you also notice a swollen tummy, less appetite, or weight loss you can't explain

These don't mean something is wrong, but they're worth checking — period pain that's new,
different, or hard to manage can have causes a clinician can help with.
period-pain.red_flags:
- Ask for an **urgent** GP appointment or call **NHS 111** if your period or pelvic pain is
  **severe, or worse than usual, and painkillers have not helped.**

premenstrual-syndrome.title: PMS (premenstrual syndrome)
premenstrual-syndrome.glance: PMS is the mix of physical and emotional changes many people notice in the week or two before a period.
premenstrual-syndrome.overview:
PMS — premenstrual syndrome — is the name for the changes many people feel in the days or couple of
weeks before their period. It can affect anyone who has periods, and it usually eases within a few
days after the period starts.

The changes come in many forms. Physically, you might notice bloating, sore or tender breasts,
cramps, headaches, or feeling more tired. Emotionally, there can be mood swings, irritability,
anxiety, or feeling low. Food cravings and changes in sleep are common too. Not everyone gets PMS,
and those who do won't get every symptom — your own pattern is what matters.

PMS is a normal, recognised part of many people's cycles, tied to the natural hormonal shifts of
the second half. Noticing how it shows up for you, cycle to cycle, can make it easier to plan
around — and to spot if it ever changes.
premenstrual-syndrome.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth talking to a GP if:

- your symptoms are affecting your daily life — work, studies, relationships
- everyday changes to your routine haven't helped
- your low mood, anxiety, or irritability feels severe

A clinician can talk through what might help. A more intense form, called premenstrual dysphoric
disorder (PMDD), can cause much stronger mood symptoms, and support is available for it.
premenstrual-syndrome.red_flags:
- If you have symptoms of PMDD and are **feeling suicidal or that you cannot keep yourself safe**,
  get help straight away: **call 999 or go to A&E.** Don't drive yourself — ask someone to take
  you, or ask for an ambulance. You deserve support, and help is available.

progesterone.title: Progesterone
progesterone.glance: Progesterone is the hormone of the cycle's second half, preparing the womb lining after ovulation.
progesterone.overview:
Progesterone is one of the main hormones behind the menstrual cycle, and it takes the lead in the
second half — after an egg is released at ovulation.

Its main role is to help the lining of the uterus (womb) stay thick and ready, so that if a
fertilised egg arrives it can implant and a pregnancy can begin. In this way progesterone works as
a partner to estrogen, which did much of the build-up earlier in the cycle.

If no pregnancy begins, progesterone levels fall. That drop is what allows the lining to be shed
as your next period. The rise and fall of progesterone across the second half of the cycle is a
normal, expected rhythm.
progesterone.deep:
Progesterone is produced mainly by the corpus luteum — the structure the ovary forms from the
follicle after it has released its egg. This is why progesterone rises specifically in the luteal
(post-ovulation) phase. When the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone and estrogen both fall,
signalling the start of a new cycle. Its natural shifts are part of why some people notice
premenstrual changes in the days before a period.

spotting.title: Spotting & bleeding between periods
spotting.glance: Spotting is light bleeding between periods or after sex — often not serious, but always worth getting checked.
spotting.overview:
Spotting means light bleeding that happens between your periods or after sex, outside your normal
flow. It's common, and it's usually not something serious — but because it can have several causes,
it's the kind of thing that's always worth getting checked by a clinician.

There are many everyday reasons for it. Starting or using hormonal contraception is a frequent one.
Others include small, harmless growths in or around the womb (polyps or fibroids), harmless changes
to the surface of the cervix, vaginal dryness, or an infection such as chlamydia.

Because the same symptom can come from different causes — most of them minor — the useful step
isn't to guess, it's to have it looked at so you know what's behind it for you.
spotting.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP or a sexual health clinic **any time you have bleeding between periods or after sex**,
  even if it's light. It's usually nothing serious, but getting it checked is how the cause is
  found — and it's the way to rule out less common causes early.
spotting.red_flags:
- Ask for an **urgent** GP appointment or call **NHS 111** if you have **missed a period and have
  unusual bleeding along with tummy or pelvic pain** — this needs prompt assessment, as it can be a
  sign of an ectopic pregnancy.
